title: Strangers
tomorrow: is there a way to pray for someone you can't stand yet?

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith at work that sounds like small, plain truths: quietly faithful. Today, the people at work, on the bus, at the counter, whose names we'll never learn.

A line out the door, the register beeping, and a woman at the counter who is new in town and in no hurry at all. She wants to know where the library is. Then what the town's like. Then whether it's always this hot. There's a verse for exactly this moment, and it doesn't say the line doesn't matter. It says something stranger about who might be standing at the counter.
screen: `A LINE OUT THE DOOR.` → `A STRANGER IN NO HURRY.` → `WHO'S AT THE COUNTER?`

segments.voice: The letter to the Hebrews says it plainly: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.” You've met this verse before, so sit with its last word. Unawares. The hosts didn't know. They welcomed a stranger, and only later was there more to the story. Genesis has a scene like it: three men appear by Abraham's tent in the heat of the day, and “when he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door.” He ran. Jesus tells a parable with the same twist. The king says, “I was a stranger, and ye took me in,” and the people are puzzled: “When saw we thee a stranger, and took thee in?” They hadn't known either. Under all of it sits a line Paul spoke to a crowd in Athens: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth.” One blood. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in both stories, the welcome comes first and the recognition comes later, if at all. Hospitality in the Bible can mean a bed and a meal. On a busy day it can be smaller: eye contact, a real answer, an invitation to come back when it's quiet. Small, but not nothing.
screen: `UNAWARES: THEY DIDN'T KNOW.` · `ABRAHAM RAN TO MEET THEM.` · `WHEN SAW WE THEE?` · `ONE BLOOD, ALL NATIONS.` · then, large: `ANGELS UNAWARES.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let one stranger from this week come back to mind: a cashier, a driver, someone at a bus stop. See their face as clearly as you can, without deciding anything about them. If you pray, simply hold them there; if not, wish them a good evening, wherever they are.
Strangers. People we don't know yet, welcomed first, the way Abraham ran to meet his guests.
Your line: angels unawares. The welcome comes first, and the knowing comes later, if ever. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians practice hospitality in many ways: welcoming newcomers at church, hosting meals, helping refugees and travelers, and everyday patience and kindness with strangers at work and in public.
